scenarios.title: Who is on my team?
scenarios.objective: Find a teammate before choosing whom to involve.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck in a sharing activity. Navy2 wears navy like you; Gold1 wears gold. The coach asks you to find your teammate. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.

questions.prompt: Who is your teammate?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is on the same navy team as YOU. The labels also identify the teams.

questions.prompt: Which two things can you find here?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is your teammate and YOU have the puck. No goal has happened.

questions.prompt: Put this sharing routine in order.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine. Matching jerseys alone does not make a pass safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer Navy2 without standing on Navy2.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance while keeping separate space. Other clear starting spots could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 steps between you and Navy2. What could you do?
questions.explanation: A teammate can become covered. Look again or find clearer space.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up how you found your teammate.
questions.explanation: Mention navy, the Navy2 label or the team introduction. Pointing is fine.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 reaches the puck first, what is your first new question?

options.text: Can I pass the old way?

questions.explanation: Gold1's arrival may change ownership. Naming the new owner keeps YOU from acting on the old loose-puck picture.

questions.prompt: After the pickup, which two players should YOU find?

options.text: A player who is not shown

questions.explanation: Gold1 is the pressure cue and Navy2 is the visible teammate. Seeing both helps decide whether to shield, carry, or pass.

questions.prompt: Place YOU between the puck and Navy2 with Gold1 in view.
questions.explanation: This example keeps YOU connected to Navy2 while leaving Gold1 visible. Another controlled support spot can work.

questions.prompt: Tell an adult what changed when Gold1 got closer.
questions.explanation: A useful answer names Gold1 as closer pressure and Navy2 as a teammate to find. The next puck touch should follow that new picture.

scenarios.title: A puck with nobody holding it
scenarios.objective: Tell a loose puck from a carried puck.
scenarios.briefing: The coach placed a puck in a quiet practice area. Nobody controls it yet. Navy2 waits beside the area. YOU are invited to collect it. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck is separate from both players.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck right now?
questions.explanation: The setup has no puck owner. It is between the players.

questions.prompt: What did the coach ask YOU to do?
questions.explanation: That is the instruction in the briefing.

questions.prompt: Arrange a gentle collection try.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested practice sequence; the picture does not measure skating or control.

questions.prompt: Show a place near the puck to finish your approach.
questions.explanation: The reference approaches without going far beyond the puck. Several nearby places may suit the activity.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 reaches it first and controls it. Is it still loose?
questions.explanation: The answer follows the stated new ownership event.

questions.prompt: How could you tell the puck was waiting for someone?
questions.explanation: Point to the separate puck and notice that neither player controls it.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 blocks the upper side, what should you check next?
questions.explanation: Gold1 changed the open-side cue. A new lane or a clear pass to Navy2 may fit, but the current space decides.

questions.prompt: Which two things help you carry with your head up?
questions.explanation: Pressure and support can both move. Checking Gold1 and Navy2 keeps the carry connected to what is open now.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in a lower open lane away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example leaves the upper pressure and keeps YOU moving in a separate lane. Other clear space may work.

questions.prompt: Why is moving and looking better than racing into Gold1?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is in the straight path. Moving toward visible space while checking Navy2 can preserve puck control and a next choice.

scenarios.title: Room to carry
scenarios.objective: Notice an occupied route and a roomier practice area.
scenarios.briefing: YOU hold the puck. Gold1 is directly ahead. Navy2 waits off to one side. The coach invites you to explore the empty side away from Navy2. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is ahead of YOUR facing direction.
Navy2 occupies one side of the practice area.
The opposite side has no player.

questions.prompt: Who is directly ahead of YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is ahead in the direction YOU face.

questions.prompt: What is shown on the side away from Navy2?
questions.explanation: No player is placed on that side of the activity. Empty space does not guarantee an escape.

questions.prompt: Arrange this try at finding room.

options.text: Carry a short way and look again

questions.explanation: The routine invites another look when the situation changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into the empty practice space away from Navy2.
questions.explanation: This leaves the crowded line and the side Navy2 occupies. Other clear places may fit; a real route still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves into that empty space. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Notice the new player position instead of remembering one fixed spot.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you checked before carrying.
questions.explanation: Gold1, Navy2 or the empty ice are relevant observations. Speaking or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 covers your first angle, what should Navy2 see?

options.text: A different clear target or lane

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first window. A new angle or lane gives Navy2 a real choice if it is visible.

questions.prompt: After moving, what two players should YOU check?
questions.explanation: Navy2 decides whether a pass can be made, and Gold1 may have changed the lane. Both are needed for the next read.

questions.prompt: Place YOU on the lower side with a clear line to Navy2.
questions.explanation: This offers a lower angle around Gold1 while keeping Navy2 visible. It is one example, not a required spot.

questions.prompt: How can you show Navy2 that you are ready?
questions.explanation: Move to a clear angle and present a visible target while checking Gold1. Readiness depends on the current lane, not just standing still.

scenarios.title: From the boards to the circle
scenarios.objective: Use boards and faceoff circle to understand a practice instruction.
scenarios.briefing: YOU are near the side boards. The coach names the nearby red ring a faceoff circle and asks you to return to its middle for the next turn. Navy2 waits outside the circle. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The named circle is centred near x=20.7, y=6.7.

questions.prompt: What does the coach call the nearby red ring?
questions.explanation: The briefing names this painted ring. It is a landmark in this practice.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU starting?
questions.explanation: YOU are close to the side boundary, outside the circle centre.

questions.prompt: Arrange the return to our practice spot.

options.text: Check that the space is clear

questions.explanation: This is a suggested activity reset, not a faceoff rule or skating test.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle of that faceoff circle.
questions.explanation: The reference is the stated practice spot. The coach could accept a nearby clear place; no tactical optimality is claimed.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 stands in the middle first. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Give your partner room and follow the coach's next instruction.

questions.prompt: Point to the boards, then point to the circle.
questions.explanation: Recognizing the two named areas is the aim. A point or spoken answer is enough.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 turns toward the middle, what should YOU protect first?

options.text: The space toward the navy end

questions.explanation: Gold1 still has the puck and the navy end is the area at risk. Keep that space in view while supporting Navy2.

questions.prompt: Which two clues help YOU choose a recovery lane?

options.text: A fixed position from before the turnover

questions.explanation: The carrier and teammate positions change where help is useful. An old fixed spot cannot decide the new lane.

questions.prompt: Place YOU closer to the navy end while keeping Gold1 in front.
questions.explanation: This example recovers toward the protected end and keeps the carrier visible. Another lane may fit the moving play.

questions.prompt: What does “our job changed” mean here?
questions.explanation: Gold1 has the puck, so Navy players must help defend. YOU should turn back, watch the carrier, and use Navy2's position to choose support.

scenarios.title: Listen for the practice stop
scenarios.objective: Recognize a stated practice stop signal.
scenarios.briefing: In this practice only, one whistle means stop under control and listen. It has just sounded. YOU hold the puck; Navy2 uses a separate lane. This is not a match restart rule. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: A practice stop signal was stated.

questions.prompt: What does this practice whistle mean?
questions.explanation: The briefing defines the signal for this activity.

questions.prompt: Which things help after that signal?
questions.explanation: Listening and awareness fit the instruction. These are suggested behaviours.

questions.prompt: Order this practice stop.
questions.explanation: The picture cannot measure stopping distance or technique.

questions.prompt: Is stopping the same as skating faster?
questions.explanation: Stopping and speeding up are different actions.

questions.prompt: Now the coach invites a restart in your lane. What could you do?

options.text: Check the lane and begin gently
Assume every whistle has the same meaning

questions.explanation: Follow the new instruction. Another activity may use different signals.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up what you would listen for next.
questions.explanation: The next instruction or permission to begin is relevant. An adult can record spoken words.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 follows you, what should you look for?

options.text: A new clear angle to Navy2
The same spot even after Gold1 moves

questions.explanation: Gold1 changed the first support spot. A new angle can help Navy2 if it stays visible and separate.

questions.prompt: What two details shape your support near the net?

options.text: A promise that the pass will arrive

questions.explanation: The carrier and defender define which support space is useful. A pass remains a possibility, not a promise.

questions.prompt: Place YOU on the lower side with Navy2 in view.
questions.explanation: This example separates YOU from the crowded net-side line and keeps the carrier visible. Another clear angle can work.

questions.prompt: Why should support move when the defender moves?
questions.explanation: Gold1 can take away the first lane. Moving with the new picture gives Navy2 a better chance to see a safe option.

scenarios.title: Ready for a short pass
scenarios.objective: Recognize the invited receiver and a partner-passing setup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck for a gentle partner pass. YOU wait at an angle. Gold1 stands outside this first activity and is not challenging. No pass has happened yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is not challenging this try.

questions.prompt: Who starts with the puck?
questions.explanation: The puck is attached to Navy2.

questions.prompt: What is YOUR job in this activity?
questions.explanation: The briefing identifies YOU as the receiver.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple partner pass.

options.text: Get ready for the gentle pass

questions.explanation: This is a suggested progression. The eventual pass needs its own explicit movement; it is not shown yet.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer, leaving space between partners.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance. Other clear receiving places could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 is not ready yet. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can wait or communicate instead of forcing the activity.

questions.prompt: How could you show your partner you are ready?
questions.explanation: A clear look or simple call can help. Discuss a receiving target with the coach; no physical technique is graded.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 closes the wall side, what could you choose?

options.text: Look for Navy2 or another safe lane
Keep the puck there without looking

questions.explanation: Gold1 changed the protected side. Navy2 or another lane may help if the new route is visible.

questions.prompt: What two cues tell you where to protect?
questions.explanation: Gold1's position and the boards are visible. They help explain how to shield the puck without guessing handedness.

questions.prompt: Place YOU above the puck with Gold1 below you.
questions.explanation: This changes YOU's relationship to Gold1 and leaves Navy2 in the forward picture. It is one controlled example.

questions.prompt: How can your body help the puck?
questions.explanation: Put your body between Gold1 and the puck, then look for Navy2. The shield buys time to see a better next action.

scenarios.title: My turn to defend the goal
scenarios.objective: Recognize the goal-defending turn and nearby crease.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have a short turn defending the navy goal at the -x end. The coach names the blue area in front of the net the crease. You are a skater taking a turn, not a permanent goalie. Gold1 has the puck; Navy2 takes the next turn. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are assigned the navy goal at the -x end.
The blue area is named the crease.
Navy2 is next in the rotation.

questions.prompt: Which goal are YOU defending?

options.text: The gold goal at the +x end
The navy goal at the -x end

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns YOU the navy goal at the -x end for this turn.

questions.prompt: What did the coach call the blue area by the net?
questions.explanation: The name is given in the briefing. This identifies an area, not a crease-entry rule.

questions.prompt: Arrange our goal-defending turns.
questions.explanation: This is the declared rotation; the coach controls the swap.

questions.prompt: Which facts belong to this activity?
questions.explanation: Gold1 owns the puck and Navy2 is next. The role is shared.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 gains control of the puck. Who has it then?
questions.explanation: The answer follows the stated change of possession.

questions.prompt: How could you help Navy2 enjoy the next turn?
questions.explanation: Encouragement and room to try are useful answers. No goaltending technique is scored.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 enters your support lane, what should you do?

options.text: Move to a new lane Navy2 can see

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first lane. A new visible lane can help the carrier without crowding the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check after moving?
questions.explanation: The carrier and defender tell YOU whether the new support lane is useful. Empty ice alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Place YOU below the carrier with space between you.
questions.explanation: This example gives Navy2 separation and another angle. A different clear support place may work.

questions.prompt: Why should teammates avoid sharing one small space?
questions.explanation: Two navy players in one spot can remove room and a passing lane. Separation lets Navy2 carry and see a target.

scenarios.title: A teammate behind your shoulder
scenarios.objective: Look beyond the forward direction to find a teammate.
scenarios.briefing: YOU face the attacking end and hold the puck. Navy2 is behind your facing direction. Gold1 is ahead on the other side. The coach asks you to find Navy2 before deciding on a puck action. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 is behind that facing direction.
Finding Navy2 does not prove a pass is open.

questions.prompt: Where is Navy2 compared with the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: YOU face the attacking end while Navy2 is behind YOU.

questions.prompt: What can looking around help you find?
questions.explanation: Teammate locations and pressure are the source-supported information cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange this looking activity.

options.text: Tell the coach where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: This is the activity routine. A screen answer does not demonstrate a real shoulder check.

questions.prompt: For a second try, move YOU away from the side with Navy2.
questions.explanation: This changes the viewing relationship while leaving space. It is a practice reset, not an ideal game position.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 skates ahead of YOU. Should you keep pointing behind?
questions.explanation: Locate the teammate again when their position changes.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you might miss by only watching the puck.
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a concrete example. A spoken answer or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 closes the middle after your reception, what can you check?
questions.explanation: Gold1 changed the middle. Navy3 or open ice may give YOU another choice if the lane is clear.

questions.prompt: What two facts describe this new play?
questions.explanation: The briefing says YOU received the puck, and Gold1 is pressure ahead. Navy2 is no longer the owner.

questions.prompt: Place YOU lower and to the side with Navy3 visible.
questions.explanation: This gives YOU another view of Navy3 while keeping Gold1 in front. It is one example support position.

questions.prompt: Why can Navy3 matter after Navy2 passes?
questions.explanation: Navy3 is a visible teammate on the lower side. After receiving, YOU can use that support if Gold1 closes the middle.

scenarios.title: My partner has it now
scenarios.objective: Recognize the new puck owner after a completed partner pass.
scenarios.briefing: A gentle partner pass has finished. Navy2 controls the puck; YOU no longer do. This picture begins after reception and does not show the pass path. Leave Navy2 room while staying in the activity. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The earlier pass is stated, not animated.

questions.prompt: Who controls the puck now?
questions.explanation: The setup begins with the puck controlled by Navy2.

questions.prompt: Does this picture show the whole moving pass?
questions.explanation: The briefing limits it to the state after reception.

questions.prompt: Put these stated events in order.
questions.explanation: This is the supplied history, not an independently simulated pass.

questions.prompt: Find separate space where Navy2 can still see YOU.
questions.explanation: This gives Navy2 room and leaves a visible partner. Other clear places may fit.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 asks for a return target. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can stay involved by getting available. A return pass still needs a clear route.

questions.prompt: What changed for YOU when the pass finished?
questions.explanation: YOU changed from having the puck to being without it. You can still help the activity.

questions.prompt: If Navy2 reaches the blue line first, what should you do?

options.text: Keep a clear space and find Navy2
Stand on the line without looking

questions.explanation: The named line is a meeting place, but Navy2's position and open space still matter. Arrive connected to the teammate.

questions.prompt: What two players matter near the meeting line?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the teammate beyond the line and Gold1 is nearby pressure. Neither the line nor an unseen player decides the play.

questions.prompt: Place YOU closer to Navy2 while keeping Gold1 below you.
questions.explanation: This example moves YOU toward the teammate and away from the lower pressure. Another clear meeting spot can work.

questions.prompt: Why is the blue line a guide instead of the answer?
questions.explanation: It gives the activity a shared landmark. YOU still need to see Navy2, Gold1, and the open lane before carrying or passing.

scenarios.title: A mistake and another try
scenarios.objective: Respond kindly to a teammate error while noticing possession.
scenarios.briefing: In a friendly keep-away activity, Navy2 missed a pass and Gold1 gained the puck. The picture starts after that change. Navy2 looks to YOU for encouragement; the coach invites everyone to keep trying. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Everyone is invited to try again.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the missed pass?
questions.explanation: The current owner and stated event both identify Gold1.

questions.prompt: Which words could encourage Navy2?
questions.explanation: These are supportive examples. Other kind words may work too.

questions.prompt: Arrange one helpful response.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine, not the only acceptable order for showing support.

questions.prompt: For the next reset, find separate practice space near Navy2.
questions.explanation: This keeps YOU involved without occupying another player. It is a reset, not a defensive answer key.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU miss the next pass. What could help?
questions.explanation: A mistake can lead to another supported attempt.

questions.prompt: Say one kind thing you would like a teammate to tell you.
questions.explanation: Any respectful encouraging answer is welcome. An adult can record the child's own words.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 controls the loose puck, what should navy players do first?

options.text: Read Gold1 and protect the navy end
Try a new touch after checking the puck

questions.explanation: Gold1 becoming the owner changes the role picture. Navy players should read the new carrier before choosing how to defend.

questions.prompt: What two clues shape the recovery after the miss?
questions.explanation: The puck state is loose and Gold1 is nearby pressure. The old pass did not complete, so it cannot guide the next touch.

questions.prompt: Place YOU beside the puck with Navy2 below you.
questions.explanation: This approaches the loose puck and keeps Navy2 in the support picture. Another controlled spot can work.

questions.prompt: What does “another try” mean after a missed pass?
questions.explanation: It means read the new loose puck, pressure, and support before trying again. Repeating the old pass without checking ignores Gold1's position.

scenarios.title: Find the loose puck and a friend
scenarios.objective: Find a loose puck, notice pressure, and choose a nearby teammate after the pickup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. YOU are skating toward a loose puck near the side boards. Navy2 is in the middle with room. Gold1 is coming from below. The coach asks you to look while you approach, then choose what helps.
cues: The puck is loose near the boards.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck now?
questions.explanation: The puck is loose, so nobody owns it yet. Find it before planning the next touch.

questions.prompt: What should you notice as you go to the puck?

options.text: A goal that has already happened

questions.explanation: Gold1 is pressure near the approach, and Navy2 is a possible support player. Looking at both keeps the next touch connected to the play.

questions.prompt: Place YOU near the loose puck, with room to see Gold1.
questions.explanation: This spot brings YOU near the puck while leaving a little view of Gold1. It is one controlled approach example; another nearby spot can work.

questions.prompt: Put this puck pickup read in order.
questions.explanation: First find the puck, then notice the nearby players, then choose the next action. Looking while approaching keeps the read current.

questions.prompt: Gold1 gets closer while you approach. What is a good update?
